title: Slicing sound and motion into data
introduction: This week's art class traced a single idea through a century of media history: the moment continuous reality — sound, motion, even a nuclear explosion — gets sliced into discrete, measurable data. We moved from speech and galloping horses to high-speed photography and the fast Fourier transform, and every step showed how that slicing reshapes what we can perceive and what art can do.
related_work: The thread began with sound and information. Homer Dudley's work on speech showed you do not need to copy the whole voice, only extract its key parts and let the receiver rebuild the rest, while Claude Shannon's information theory separated the mechanism of transmission from the meaning it carries — the move that made digitising sound possible. Early motion capture did the same to movement: Eadweard Muybridge's cameras split a galloping horse into a sequence of stills, and Étienne-Jules Marey's photographic gun turned bird flight into measurable, repeatable data and laid the ground for cinema. Harold Edgerton pushed this further with high-speed photography, catching a bullet through an apple or a falling drop of milk, and was later commissioned by the US Department of Energy to slice the instant of a nuclear blast into millionths of a second. Artists answered in kind: Marcel Duchamp's Nude Descending a Staircase folded Marey's time slices into one picture, while Picasso's cubism rebuilt space, and Trevor Paglen's photographs of Yosemite point back to the early landscape photographers who also mapped land for the military, exposing the link between photography and military expansion. Finally, the fast Fourier transform — first used to tell Soviet underground nuclear tests from earthquakes — became the quiet foundation of scientific imaging, biomedicine, deep-space work and electronic music, and Leif Inge used it to stretch Beethoven's Ninth from ninety minutes into a twenty-four-hour piece, unchanged in pitch.
method: I approached the lecture as a chain rather than a list. Instead of memorising each inventor, I asked what the same gesture did each time: taking something continuous and turning it into frames, bits or frequencies, then asking who or what was left out and what new way of seeing it made possible.
results_discussion: What came through most clearly is that this is not just a technical story. Slicing the world into data keeps changing what counts as real and visible: a voice becomes reusable parts, a run becomes frames, and a nuclear instant becomes a millionth-of-a-second slice that could also trigger a detonator. The artists are not separate from this — Duchamp and Picasso showed that the same slicing could be bent toward seeing time and space differently, and Paglen reminds us that the camera has always been tangled up with military expansion. Leif Inge's twenty-four-hour Beethoven was the moment it clicked for me: the same transform that separates earthquakes from bomb tests can also stretch our sense of time, so the shift from analogue to digital is really a reshaping of how we perceive time and space.
conclusion_future_work: My takeaway is that every time a technology turns something continuous into data, it changes what we can sense — and what we might be missing. That matters for my own work with sensors, because a sensor is exactly that kind of cut. Going forward I want to ask, for each measurement I make, what the measurement leaves out, the same question the artists in this lecture kept asking.
